platforms.title: A1C vs. Fasting Glucose: Why Do the Two Tests Disagree?
platforms.meta_description: An A1C in the prediabetes range next to a normal fasting glucose is common, not a lab error. Here is what each test measures and what to do next.
platforms.body_html:
You fasted, had blood drawn, and the fasting glucose came back normal — then the same panel showed an A1C of 5.9 percent — a value NIDDK guidelines place squarely in the prediabetes band. It reads like a contradiction, but it is a common and well-documented one: the two tests are not measuring the same thing over the same stretch of time. Here is what each number actually reports, why they can point in different directions, and what the evidence says is worth doing next.

What the A1C Is Actually Measuring

Hemoglobin is the protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen, and glucose in the bloodstream binds to it. The more glucose circulating, the more hemoglobin ends up carrying it. The A1C test measures that share, which is why the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) describes it as reflecting average blood glucose over the past 3 months rather than a single moment. No fasting is required, and blood can be drawn at any time of day.

On the ranges NIDDK publishes for diagnosis, a normal A1C is below 5.7 percent, 5.7 to 6.4 percent is prediabetes, and 6.5 percent or above is diabetes. Two conditions travel with those numbers and are easy to miss. The sample has to go to a lab using an NGSP-certified method — fingerstick point-of-care devices are explicitly not for diagnosis — and any test used to diagnose needs a second confirming measurement unless clear symptoms are present.

Why Your Fasting Glucose and A1C Disagree

NIDDK states it plainly: a blood glucose test can show diabetes when an A1C does not, and an A1C can indicate diabetes when a blood glucose test does not. Fasting glucose is a snapshot that moves with what you ate the night before, how you slept, illness, and stress. The A1C is much less sensitive to those short-term swings. When the two disagree, NIDDK notes that a person may simply be at an early stage, when glucose has not risen high enough to show up on every test — which is why clinicians often follow closely and repeat the test in several months rather than declaring the normal result the winner.

The A1C also has documented blind spots, and they matter more than most reports let on. Anything that changes red blood cell lifespan — recent blood loss, transfusion, hemodialysis, sickle cell disease — shifts the number, and iron-deficiency anemia can push it falsely high. For people of African, Mediterranean, or Southeast Asian descent, a hemoglobin variant can interfere with some A1C assays, which is worth naming out loud at the appointment. Even the test's own precision leaves room: NIDDK notes an A1C reported as 6.8 percent could come back anywhere from 6.4 to 7.2 percent on a repeat run of the same blood sample.

What Happens When You Act on a Prediabetes Range

This is the part worth sitting with, because the numbers here are unusually good. In the Diabetes Prevention Program, adults at high risk who joined an intensive lifestyle program — aiming for 7 percent body weight loss and 150 minutes of exercise per week — had a 58 percent lower chance of developing type 2 diabetes than the placebo group after about three years. That figure is a comparison against placebo in a high-risk population over three years, not a general promise, but it is the strongest signal in this whole area.

  • 5 to 7 percent of your starting weight — NIDDK's everyday version of the DPP target. At 200 pounds that is roughly 10 to 14 pounds, not a transformation.
  • 30 minutes, 5 days a week — NIDDK's floor for physical activity. Walking counts, and splitting it into shorter blocks is fine.
  • More fiber from food, with honest expectations — a 2020 systematic review in PLOS Medicine pooled 33 trials of increasing fiber intake in adults with prediabetes or diabetes and found HbA1c fell by about 2 mmol/mol, roughly 0.2 percentage points, versus control. Real, but modest on its own, which is exactly why it belongs alongside weight and activity rather than instead of them.

Two safety notes. If you already take a glucose-lowering medication or insulin, do not change the dose or stop it because a diet or exercise plan is going well — that decision belongs to the prescriber, who can adjust as your numbers move. And learn the signs of low blood sugar: shakiness, sweating, confusion, a racing heart. If someone becomes unable to swallow safely, has a seizure, or loses consciousness, that is an emergency — call 911 rather than waiting it out.

The One Thing to Remember

If you keep only one line from this: a normal fasting glucose does not overrule an A1C in the 5.7 to 6.4 percent band. Ask for the confirming test instead of assuming the reassuring number is the accurate one, and use the window it buys you. This article is general health information, not medical advice or a diagnosis — bring your actual lab report to a clinician who can read both numbers together.
